A cheerless fellow. Some people find him an intolerable companion. I was talking at dinner in London a few nights ago to a woman who has a house in Sussex, and I found that she had not been there for some time.

"I used to find the owl endurable," said she, "but since the war I have found him unbearable. He hoots all night and makes me so depressed that I feel that I shall go mad."

"And so you come and listen to the owl in London?" I said.

"The owl in London?" she asked.

"Yes," I said, "the owl that hoots in Carmelite Street and Printing House Square."

"Ah," she said, "but he is such an absurd owl. Now the owl down in the country is such a solemn creature."

I murmured.

"Yes, but in the silence and the darkness there doesn't seem any answer to him."

"Madame," I said, "if you will look up at the stars you will find a very complete answer."

I confess that I find the owl not only tolerable but stimulating. I like to hear the pessimist really let himself go. It is the nameless and unformed fears of the mind that paralyse, but when my owl comes along and states the position at its blackest I begin to cheer up and feel defiant and combative. Is this the worst that can be said? Then let us see what the best is, and set about accomplishing it. "The thing is impossible," said the pessimist to Cobden. "Indeed," said that great man. "Then the sooner we set about doing it the better." Oh, oh, say I to my owl, all is lost, is it? You wait till the dawn comes, and hear what that little chap in the red waistcoat has to say about it. message.content:
A gloomy individual. Many consider him an unbearable presence. Recently, while dining in London, I conversed with a woman who owns a house in Sussex, and I learned that she hadn’t visited it in quite a while.

"I used to tolerate the owl," she remarked, "but ever since the war, he has become insufferable. He hoots throughout the night, leaving me so despondent that I feel I might lose my sanity."

"So, you prefer the owl in London, then?" I inquired.

"The owl in London?" she replied, sounding puzzled.

"Yes," I continued, "the owl that hoots in Carmelite Street and Printing House Square."

"Ah," she acknowledged, "but that owl is rather ridiculous. The one back in the countryside, however, has a more serious demeanor."

"He expresses very foolish ideas with such gravity," I interjected softly.

"True, but in the stillness of the night, it feels as if there’s no response to his lamentations."

"My dear lady," I countered, "if you simply gaze up at the stars, you will find a very thorough reply."

I must admit that I not only find the owl bearable but also invigorating. Hearing a pessimist articulate their bleak outlook can actually inspire me. It is the vague and undefined anxieties that immobilize us; however, when my owl articulates the situation in its most dire form, I begin to feel uplifted, emboldened, and ready for a challenge. If this is the worst possible scenario, then let’s discover what the best can be and strive to achieve it. "That task is impossible," the pessimist once told Cobden. "Oh really?" Cobden replied. "Then we should embark on it at once." How interesting, I think to my owl, so all is lost, is it? Just wait until dawn arrives, and listen to what that little fellow in the red waistcoat has to say. He has a completely different narrative to share, one that is far more plausible than your dismal tale. I’ll head off to bed now, leaving you to your dreary thoughts until the sun rises to reveal just how mistaken you truly are.
